clue.text: Formal apparel vested in America

parts.note: the clue describes evening dress for men under its American name, with 'vested' hinting at being clothed

explanation.surface: A ceremonial outfit, or a right formally granted to the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vested' reads as a legal term (power vested in someone) but here means clothed: the evening jacket named after Tuxedo Park, New York.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call a dinner jacket by this name, after the New York club where it became fashionable.

clue.text: Drink horse, we hear, has gone crazy about

indicators.note: the scrambled letters sit around the horse, so 'about' signals one piece enclosing the other
'gone crazy' tells us the letters of gone are jumbled into a new order
the phrase tells us the horse is spoken, its sound giving two letters

parts.note: gee-gee is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: A drinking horse that has lost its mind, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' tempts you toward a drink like a horse's neck, but the horse is the nursery gee-gee. 'Has' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a festive beverage of eggs, milk and often spirits.

clue.text: Find the lady, say, in the con-man's repertoire

definitions.text: Find the lady, say, in the con-man's repertoire

parts.words: Find the lady, say, in the con-man's repertoire
parts.note: find the lady is the three-card swindle, a literal trick a con man knows, and the phrase also means any professional knack

explanation.surface: A street hustler's stock of swindles includes the three-card game.
explanation.walkthrough: Find the lady (three-card monte) is a card trick, and a con man's trade is swindling, so it is literally one of his trade's tricks.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a clever professional knack, here a cardsharp's swindle.

clue.text: Showing affection in public transport?

explanation.surface: Kissing on the bus.
explanation.definitionFit: To buss is an old word for to kiss, and bussing is also carrying people by coach.

clue.text: Brilliant king looking men, tally deranged. (Lear, perhaps)

definitions.note: Shakespeare's king is an example of someone in this state; the definition names a person, the answer describes him

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
read together, men and tally make mentally, so the phrase reads as mentally deranged, meaning insane

explanation.surface: A dazzling monarch glaring at his men, his count of them confused, like Shakespeare's tragic king.
explanation.walkthrough: The last piece hides 'mentally deranged' across the comma, which gives MAD. Lear, perhaps, is an example of someone thus described.
explanation.definitionFit: King Lear goes completely insane on the heath in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Propositions assumed for building

explanation.surface: Assumptions made for construction work.
explanation.definitionFit: Premises are the starting propositions of an argument, and also a property or building.

clue.text: Sounds near to losin' one's nerve in a small vessel

indicators.note: the phrase says the answer is pronounced almost like the words that follow

parts.note: losing one's nerve is panicking, here with its final g dropped as the apostrophe shows

explanation.surface: Someone losing courage aboard a little boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g in 'losin'' tells you to drop it from panicking too: PANICKIN'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pannikin is a small metal drinking cup.

clue.text: Young lady of Germany in peak form

explanation.surface: A German girl looking her best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In peak form' sounds like good condition; 'peak' is the Swiss mountain. 'In' and 'form' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: The German word means maiden, and it is also a famous Alpine mountain.

clue.text: Sailing vessel of chequered design?

explanation.surface: A boat with a checked pattern.
explanation.definitionFit: A tartan is a single-masted Mediterranean boat and also a Scottish checked cloth pattern.

clue.text: Spring in a Belgian resort

explanation.surface: Springtime in a Belgian town.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a mineral spring, named after the Belgian town of Spa.

clue.text: Repeats a form of art scene

indicators.note: the phrase tells us the letters of art scene take another shape

explanation.surface: Copies one style of the art world.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who reenacts something does it again, staging a repeat.

clue.text: Borrow book about gipsy gentleman

explanation.surface: Taking out a book about a Romany gent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Borrow' is not 'take on loan': it is George Borrow, the 19th-century English writer, whose novel has this title. 'About' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrow's 1857 novel bears this title, which is also a Romany term for a gentleman who mixes with travellers.

clue.text: Why so altruistic, one might exclaim!

definitions.text: Why so altruistic, one might exclaim!

parts.words: Why so altruistic, one might exclaim!
parts.note: an exasperated exclamation, read literally, asks for the benefit of kindness itself

explanation.surface: An exasperated question to a do-gooder.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is an exasperated oath, which literally means acting for the benefit of virtue.

clue.text: See 12
Service that could be given anytime

indicators.note: the phrase says the word anytime may be reworked into something else

explanation.surface: A service available at any hour.
explanation.definitionFit: An amenity is a useful facility or service provided.

clue.text: Edgy, and could be alarming

indicators.note: the phrase says the letters of alarming can form another word

explanation.surface: Nervous, and possibly frightening.
explanation.definitionFit: Something marginal lies at the edge or border.

clue.text: Displaying the appetite of a mouse

definitions.text: Displaying the appetite of a mouse

parts.words: Displaying the appetite of a mouse
parts.note: a mouse eats in small bites, so the phrase describes taking tiny morsels

explanation.surface: Eating as little as a rodent does.
explanation.definitionFit: To take small bites, the way rodents eat, is to eat in little nips.

clue.text: An issue of clerical scratch golfers?

definitions.text: An issue of clerical scratch golfers?

parts.words: An issue of clerical scratch golfers?
parts.note: a scratch golfer plays to par and issue means offspring, so the sons of par, read as clergymen

explanation.surface: A question about children of golfing churchmen.
explanation.walkthrough: Scratch golfers play to PAR, and their issue (children) are SONS: PAR SONS, who are clerical folk.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsons are clergymen of a parish.

clue.text: Inboard propeller

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Inboard propeller' (3): OAR is hidden in 'board' with 'In' as the hidden-word indicator, but the clue prints them as one word 'Inboard', so one word is both indicator and fodder

clue.text: Natural features in a theatrical setting

explanation.surface: Landscapes on a stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Scenery is a landscape's appearance and also a stage's painted backdrop.

clue.text: Mathematicians in the making, possibly

parts.note: young people who solve sums would be children of problems, read literally

explanation.surface: Children who may grow up to be mathematicians.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually means difficult youngsters; here it reads as children who work on problems.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means troublesome youngsters, here taken literally as young problem-solvers.

clue.text: Elaborate on part of the painting

explanation.surface: Explaining one section of a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To detail is to describe fully, and a detail is a small section of an artwork.

clue.text: He who loves and runs away with another

definitions.text: He who loves and runs away with another

parts.words: He who loves and runs away with another
parts.note: this echoes the proverb about fighting and running away, describing a lover who flees to marry

explanation.surface: A twist on the saying about fighting and running away.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who runs off secretly to marry their lover elopes.

clue.text: Land worker handy in a boat

explanation.surface: A farmhand who is useful on a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handy' sounds like useful; it means the handle that steers a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmer tills the soil, and a boat's steering handle has this name.

clue.text: Refusal for example in a race

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the word for race, so in signals placement within

parts.note: a nation is a people or race

explanation.surface: A refusal at some sporting contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying no is a denial or contradiction of what is offered.

clue.text: Tea-brewing goddess

indicators.note: something brewing is being mixed and stirred, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A deity making a pot of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Ate personified folly and ruin.

clue.text: Commonly drunk, it is recorded

explanation.surface: A drunk being recorded.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses canned for intoxicated, and canned laughter or music is pre-recorded.

clue.text: Sold for cash and finds dealer is crooked

indicators.note: something crooked is bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dishonest trader sells up and gets found out.
explanation.definitionFit: Assets converted into money are said to have been realised.
